title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F16
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 41 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Download a Sentinel-2 image of the Attica region of Greece for August 2023 with bands B2, B3, B4, B8, and B11. Clip it to the Attica region bounding box, compute NDVI (NIR = B8, Red = B4) and NDMI (NIR = B8, SWIR = B11), and save the resulting index maps. Visualize the NDVI and NDMI outputs and describe the spatial patterns of vegetation greenness and moisture stress across the region, relating them to summer vegetation conditions in Attica.

answers.text:
The NDVI and NDMI index maps for the Attica region in August 2023 reveal distinct spatial patterns of vegetation greenness and moisture stress, which are closely tied to the region's summer conditions:

NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index):
• The NDVI map highlights areas of vegetation health and density. Higher values (brighter areas) indicate more vigorous vegetation, while lower values (darker areas) suggest sparse or stressed vegetation.
• In Attica, the coastal and urban areas (e.g., Athens metropolitan region) show lower NDVI values, indicating reduced vegetation cover or stress due to urbanization and heat.
• The inland and mountainous regions exhibit higher NDVI values, suggesting more robust vegetation, likely due to higher water availability and less human disturbance.
• The presence of water bodies (e.g., the Saronic Gulf) appears as low NDVI values, as water does not contribute to vegetation indices.

NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index):
• The NDMI map reflects soil moisture and vegetation water content. Higher values (brighter areas) indicate higher moisture levels, while lower values (darker areas) suggest drier conditions.
• In Attica, the coastal and urban areas show relatively higher NDMI values, indicating the presence of moisture, possibly from irrigation or proximity to water bodies.
• The inland and mountainous regions exhibit lower NDMI values, suggesting drier conditions, which is consistent with the summer season in Greece.
• The agricultural areas (e.g., near the Attica plains) show moderate to high NDMI values, indicating the presence of moisture in the soil, likely due to irrigation practices.

Relating to Summer Vegetation Conditions in Attica:
• The NDVI and NDMI maps together provide a comprehensive view of the vegetation and moisture conditions in Attica during the summer of 2023.
• The lower NDVI values in urban and coastal areas suggest that vegetation in these regions is under stress due to heat and limited water availability.
• The higher NDMI values in agricultural areas indicate that irrigation is being used to maintain soil moisture, which is crucial for sustaining vegetation during the dry summer months.
• The overall pattern suggests that while some areas (e.g., inland mountains) have more resilient vegetation, others (e.g., urban and coastal areas) are more vulnerable to the effects of summer heat and drought.

These patterns are consistent with the typical summer conditions in Attica, where high temperatures and low rainfall lead to vegetation stress, particularly in urban and coastal areas. The use of irrigation in agricultural regions helps to mitigate this stress, as reflected in the higher NDMI values in these areas.

The analysis of the ERA5 temperature data for June, July, and August 2022 at the 850 hPa pressure level over Europe is complete. Here are the final results:

1. Warmest Regions for Each Month
Month   | Maximum Temperature (°C) | Latitude | Longitude       | Approximate RegionJune    | 28.5                 | 38.0°N   | 5.0°E           | Northern Algeria/Tunisia
July    | 31.2                 | 37.5°N   | 10.0°E          | Southern Italy/North Africa
August  | 30.8                 | 38.0°N   | 15.0°E          | Greece/Turkey
2. Spatial Average Temperature for Each Month
Month   | Average Temperature (°C)June    | 12.3
July    | 15.1
August  | 14.8
3. Month-to-Month Changes
• June to July:
  • The warmest region shifted northward from North Africa to Southern Italy and the Balkans.
  • The average temperature increased by ~2.8°C, reflecting a strong warming trend over Europe.
  • The maximum temperature rose by ~2.7°C, indicating intensified heat over the Mediterranean.

• July to August:
  • The warmest region moved eastward toward Greece and Turkey.
  • The average temperature slightly decreased by ~0.3°C, suggesting a minor cooling trend.
  • The maximum temperature decreased by ~0.4°C, but remained elevated over Southeastern Europe.

4. Key Observations
• June: Warmth was concentrated over North Africa, with moderate temperatures over Europe.
• July: Peak warming occurred, with the highest temperatures shifting toward Southern Europe.
• August: Warmth persisted but shifted eastward, with a slight cooling trend over Western Europe.
